units: a wall painting decays because its support soaks up water
the coloured layer lifts off the wall in flakes
the damage comes from the support and not from the coloured matter
the first step is to draw the damp out of the wall
compresses pull the salts out of the wall
the loosened fragments are refixed with a liquid adhesive
the losses are filled with fine hatching that shows up close to
the missing decoration is not put back by repainting
text: Picture a painted wall flaking away in front of you. The plaster drinks in the damp, the colour lifts, and the wall painting that a workshop once laid down there ends up as dust. The blame rarely sits with the pigment itself; it is the support underneath that moves. So conservators begin by drying the wall out, gently, with compresses that pull the salt out of it. Then they refix the flakes one by one, slipping a liquid adhesive behind every lifted fragment. The brush arrives last, and even then it mainly serves to settle the gaps with fine hatching that you notice only close to. No serious workshop repaints what has gone: they fill, they steady the surface, they leave the loss on show. What you get is a painting that stands up and owns its wounds instead of hiding them under make-up.

units: an exhibition splits the finished work and its preparatory drawings between two rooms
the finished painting hangs alone on a dark wall
visitors lower their voices in front of the finished painting
the preparatory drawings hang close together and show changes of mind
the public stops for longer in front of the preparatory drawings
the preparatory drawings get visitors talking to one another
a teacher reckons her pupils grasp at last how gradual the making of art is
the organiser of the exhibition hesitated before showing the working documents
text: The contrast hit you the moment you walked in. In the first room the finished canvas hung alone on a dark wall, lit like a relic, and visitors dropped their voices in front of it. In the second, the preparatory drawings were pinned up close together, changes of mind and all, hesitant lines, thumbprints from the painter. The attendants say the crowd lingers far longer over the drawings. The finished work commands silence; the working sheets set people talking to one another. A teacher who had come with her class put it plainly: her pupils grasped at last that an image does not arrive whole from an inspired mind, but gropes about, fails and starts again. The organiser of the show admits he hesitated before opening that second room, for fear of stripping the mystery from what he was showing.

units: the modelling material has to be softened under the hands first
the air bubbles are driven out by slamming the lump on a hard surface
a dull sound tells you the air has gone
the thumbs hollow the piece out from the centre
the fingers draw the wall upwards
drying happens in the shade under a damp cloth
draughts are to be avoided while the piece dries
the cut base has to be wider than the piece
a plaster cast lets you copy the shape once the surface is dry
text: Start by waking the clay up. It comes out of the bag cold and closed; worked slowly under the palms, it softens and stops fighting back. Then there is the air to deal with. Slam the lump down onto a hard, unyielding surface, again and again, until the sound turns dull and flat, which tells you the air has gone. Shaping follows immediately: the thumbs hollow out from the centre while the fingers draw the wall upwards. Drying is the thankless stage that impatience invariably ruins. Keep the piece in the shade under a damp cloth that slows the water leaving, and well away from draughts. Last of all comes the base, cut wider than the piece itself, because anything standing needs an honest footing. If you want a copy of your model, make a plaster cast, but wait until the surface is dry to the touch.

units: the window was taken down panel by panel
every element was placed on a measured drawing before it came out
the glass was washed in demineralised water at the workshop
the washing had to spare the dark painted layer
the broken glass was bonded with resin under a magnifying instrument
resin bonding cannot be undone afterwards
a second window was fitted in front of the original to shield it from swings in heat
the new metalwork is finer than the one before
the refitting has to be over before the cold season
text: The undertaking opened with the removal of the window, panel by panel, each piece marked on a measured drawing before it was eased out of its leadwork. The glass then travelled to the workshop, where washing in demineralised water lifted the sulphate deposits without touching the dark painted layer. The most delicate operation followed: bonding the broken glass with resin under a magnifying instrument, a step that cannot be reversed later on. Those directing the site then settled on protective outer glazing, a second window set in front of the original to shield it from swings in heat and from condensation. Rebuilding came after that, with fresh metalwork narrower than the old, so that the drawing could be read again. The refitting will be over before the cold season, the client body says.

units: the performance hall sits on the top floor of an old building
its timber frame is left in view
the wood soaks up part of the lower notes and takes the edge off harsh tones
the side walls lean in slightly
the lean of the walls throws the sound back towards the middle rows
listeners at the back hear almost as well as those at the front
the low ceiling cuts the reverberation short
spoken voices come across more clearly while large ensembles lose their fullness
the place mostly programmes small groups and readings
text: The hall occupies the top floor of an old building, and its exposed timber frame decides how it sounds. Wood resonates with the lower notes, so it soaks up part of the energy in the room and takes the edge off the harsher timbres. The side walls lean in a little, which throws the reflections back towards the middle rows; anyone at the back hears almost as well as those in the front. The low ceiling, on the other hand, cuts the reverberation abruptly short. Spoken voices come across cleanly, while large ensembles lose their fullness. The programming follows directly from all that. Small ensembles, recitals and readings are what the place invites, and the heavy forces that the volume could never carry without muddle are quietly left aside. Here the architecture itself dictates the repertoire.

units: the greater part of museum collections stays out of the display rooms
a shortage of space and of funding explains this
one answer is to digitise the stored holdings on a large scale
digitising makes a piece shut in a drawer visible from a distance
another answer is to lend works out for a limited time
these loans benefit institutions that cannot afford to buy pieces
the writer holds that both answers have to be pursued together
the two answers meet different needs
text: Museum stores hold the vast bulk of what our collections contain, and that bulk never leaves its crates. The imbalance is hardly a secret: only a sliver of what is kept ever goes on show, for want of floor space, of staff and of funding. Two possible remedies are being aired. The first is to digitise on a considerable scale, so that a print shut in a drawer becomes something anyone can consult from a screen. The second is to move works about on temporary loan, towards smaller institutions with no budget for acquisitions. Both deserve to be pursued together, because they answer different needs: one feeds study and curiosity from a distance, the other offers a meeting in the flesh with the object. Refusing to choose between them is costly. Leaving a whole heritage asleep costs a good deal more.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the craftsman compares his trade to a discipline of patience
he used to draw on a screen
a mistake made on a screen was undone without consequence
the metal he engraves allows no correction
that constraint has made him more demanding, he says
on the screen he worked fast and dropped his difficult ideas
on the plate he thinks before every cut
a cut taken too deep destroys weeks of effort
his daughter is learning to draw on a computer and teases him about his method
text: The engraver in the back workshop talks about his trade as a sport of patience. He used to draw on a screen, where a mistake disappeared at a keystroke and cost him nothing. Since he took up a burin, everything has changed. Copper forgives nothing, he says, laughing, and that is exactly what has made him better. He readily compares the two practices. On the screen he turned out work quickly and in quantity, but he dropped an idea the moment it put up a fight. On the plate he thinks before every cut, because one line taken too deep obliterates weeks of effort. His daughter, who is learning to draw on a computer, teases him and calls him a cave-dwelling craftsman. He tells her he will teach her engraving when she learns to wait, and that she will see then that slowness is a method, not a punishment.

units: the writer picks out three successes and one fault in this exhibition
the low picture rails force the visitor to step in close
that closeness changes how the small formats are seen
the labels are short and free of jargon
the labels set out a technique instead of commenting on a feeling
a quiet sound track plays workshop noises
these noises stand in for ambient music
the lighting is too even and flattens the ridges of thick paint
the writer advises a visit late in the afternoon when the sun comes in through the high windows
text: Three things save this show, and one thing weighs it down. The arrangement comes first: the picture rails have been hung low, so you have to step in close, and that closeness transforms what the intimate formats do to you. Then the labels, written short and mercifully free of jargon, which set out how a thing was made instead of telling you what to feel. Then the sound, kept low, a knife scraping across a palette, an easel creaking as it is shifted: the noise of the work itself, worth immeasurably more than any ambient music. The fault lies in the lighting, too uniform throughout, flattening the ridges of paint on the most heavily loaded pieces. It would be worth returning late in the afternoon, when low sun reaches in through the high windows, to catch what the arrangement failed to bring out.

units: the writer is writing from a performance hall that is still empty
he turned up late to his first class in the autumn
he had sworn never to go back on stage
he came back every week through the cold season
he kept it up out of stubbornness first and then for the pleasure of it
the head of the company gave him the part of an old caretaker
that part says little and watches the others
the performance the night before played to a full house
the person he writes to had urged him to sign up for the class
the writer invites him to the last performance
text: I am writing from the empty auditorium, before the others arrive. Do you remember my first class, back in the autumn? I arrived late with my coat still on, and I swore I would never set foot on that stage again. The cold months went by and I kept coming back every week, out of stubbornness at first, then because I enjoyed it. When the stage sessions began, the head of the company handed me the part of the old caretaker, the one who says little and watches everyone. Last night we played to a full house. I felt the silence close over my first line like still water. I am not writing to boast. I am writing because you were the one who pushed me to sign up, on an evening when I claimed nothing amused me any longer. Come to the last performance; I am keeping you a seat in the front row.

units: old paper browns because of the raw material itself
pulp made from wood holds a substance that oxidises in light and air
that oxidation releases acids which break down the cellulose
the brown ringed stains come from too much damp together with spores
a fungus feeds on the size held in the sheet
washing removes those stains only in part
an alkaline bath neutralises the acids that are there
the bath leaves a protective reserve in the sheet
mounting in a sealed frame limits distortion when the work is moved
text: We are often asked what turns the paper of an old print brown. The cause lies in the fibre itself: as soon as the pulp contains wood, the lignin it contains oxidises in daylight and air, then releases acids that eat away at the cellulose. And the brown ringed stain? That comes from too much damp in the air together with spores. A fungus establishes itself, feeds on the size in the sheet and leaves a mark that washing only partly eliminates. What does a conservation workshop do once it has that diagnosis? It deacidifies in an alkaline bath, which neutralises the acids and leaves a protective buffer reserve in the sheet. And if the work has to travel? It is mounted in a neutral quality window mount inside a sealed frame, since every shift in humidity works the fibre and accentuates the cockling.
